name: Blast
summary: A fungus disease that burns rice leaves and can break the neck of the panicle (grain head), so grain is lost. It can attack at any growth stage from nursery to heading.
symptoms: Small bluish-green flecks on leaves grow into spindle-shaped spots with grey centres and dark brown edges.
Spots join together and large patches of leaf dry up, so a badly hit nursery or field looks burnt.
Black spots ring the nodes (joints) of the stem, and the stem may break at the node.
Neck of the panicle turns grayish-brown to black, shrivels, and the panicle may fall over.
Infection before the milky stage gives no grain. Later infection gives poor quality grain.
causes: Caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae (also called Pyricularia grisea); its spores are in the air through the year.
Favoured by cloudy skies, drizzle and frequent rain, wet leaves, high humidity and temperatures of about 25 to 28 degrees C.
Too much nitrogen fertilizer, dry nurseries and late planting make the disease worse.

actions.text: Check nursery and field often. Look for leaf spots at tillering and for neck infection at flowering.
Give nitrogen fertilizer in split doses and avoid applying too much at one time.
Remove weeds on bunds and field edges, which can carry the fungus.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
After harvest, clear straw and stubble from the field so the fungus does not carry over.

prevention: Grow resistant or tolerant varieties; this is the most practical and cheapest control. Ask your agriculture office which varieties suit your area.
Avoid dry nurseries and avoid planting late.
Avoid heavy nitrogen fertilizer; use split doses.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if leaf spots are spreading or if necks are turning black near flowering.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Blast

name: Sheath Blight
summary: A fungus disease of rice that starts on the leaf sheaths near the water line and climbs up the plant. Bad infection kills leaves and gives poorly filled grain.
symptoms: First spots are greenish-grey, oval or irregular, on the leaf sheath close to the water level.
Spots grow with greyish-white centres and blackish-brown or purple-brown borders.
Lesions join and spread upward from the water line towards the flag leaf (the top leaf).
Many large lesions can kill whole leaves; in severe cases the whole plant dies.
Heavy infection at heading and grain filling gives poorly filled grain, especially in the lower part of the panicle.
causes: Caused by the fungus Rhizoctonia solani, which survives as hard round brown bodies (sclerotia) in soil and floats on irrigation water.
Spreads through irrigation water; it can survive many months in soil and attacks many other plants.
Favoured by humid weather (96 to 100 percent), temperatures of 28 to 32 degrees C, frequent rain, heavy nitrogen fertilizer and close spacing or high seed rate.

actions.text: Do not let irrigation water flow from an infected field into healthy fields.
Check the crop from tillering onward, looking at the sheaths near the water line.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
After harvest, plough deeply in summer and clear stubble to reduce the fungus left in the field.

prevention: Grow moderately resistant varieties; ask your agriculture office which ones suit your area.
Avoid very close spacing and very high seed rates.
Avoid too much nitrogen fertilizer.
Add well rotted farmyard manure or other organic matter as advised locally.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if sheath lesions are climbing up the plants.

sources.title: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Sheath Blight

name: Gray Leaf Spot
summary: A fungus disease of corn leaves that makes long rectangular tan to gray spots between the veins. Heavy attack on the leaves above the ear can cut yield.
symptoms: Early spots are small brown or tan spots with yellow edges, easiest to see when the leaf is held to the light.
Older spots are tan to gray, rectangular with blunt ends, and stopped by the leaf veins.
In severe cases spots join and whole leaves, even whole plants, dry up.
Stalks may weaken and fall over in severe cases, and the field may ripen early.
causes: Caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis, which survives on corn residue lying on or above the soil and survives poorly when buried.
Spores travel by wind and rain splash to lower leaves, and can blow in from nearby fields.
Favoured by long leaf wetness, high humidity inside the crop, and moderate to warm weather.
Risk is higher with susceptible hybrids, corn grown year after year, late planting and minimum tillage.

actions.text: Walk the field and check lower leaves before flowering, especially if the field had this disease last season.
After harvest, plough or bury corn residue so the fungus has less place to survive.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
Avoid planting corn again in a field that had heavy disease; rotate to another crop.

prevention: Choose the most tolerant hybrids or varieties available; none is fully resistant.
Rotate with a crop that is not corn.
Avoid late planting.
Bury residue after a diseased crop.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spots are spreading on leaves above the ear.

sources.title: Gray Leaf Spot on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension
Gray Leaf Spot of Corn - University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension

name: Northern Leaf Blight
summary: A fungus disease that makes long canoe-shaped spots on corn leaves. It is worst in damp, moderate weather and can cause losses in susceptible varieties.
symptoms: Long canoe-shaped spots, about 1 to 6 inches long, on the leaves.
Spots start gray-green at the edges, then turn tan and may show dark fungal growth.
Spots appear first on lower leaves and then move upward.
In severe cases leaves are blighted (dried up) quickly.
causes: Caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum; there are several races that behave differently on different varieties.
The fungus survives on old corn leaf residue.
Favoured by moderate temperatures (about 64 to 80 degrees F) and long periods of moisture.
It usually shows at or after silking; earlier infection causes more damage.

actions.text: Check lower leaves for canoe-shaped spots, especially in damp weather before and around silking.
Bury or clear old corn residue after harvest, since the fungus survives on it.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
Rotate fields out of corn where the disease was heavy.

prevention: Plant resistant hybrids or varieties; this is the main control.
Rotate crops and manage residue after a diseased crop.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spots appear on many plants before silking.

sources.title: Northern Corn Leaf Blight - University of Minnesota Extension

name: Rust
summary: A fungus disease that puts rusty-brown raised pustules on corn leaves. It is usually mild but can hurt the crop in long cool, wet spells.
symptoms: Small brown pustules (raised spots) on both the upper and lower leaf surfaces, and on leaf sheaths.
Pustules are brick-red to cinnamon-brown and the powder rubs off on your fingers.
Pustules darken as they age, often with a yellow ring around them.
In severe attacks leaves turn yellow and die.
causes: Caused by the rust fungus Puccinia sorghi. Its spores are carried by wind and new spores form within 7 to 14 days.
Favoured by cool, moist weather (about 16 to 25 degrees C), heavy dew and at least 6 hours of wet leaves.
Hot, dry weather slows or stops the disease.
Young leaves are most easily infected.

actions.text: Scout fields early and often, more so if rust has been seen in nearby fields.
Note how much of the leaf is covered and how far the plants have grown, and show this to your agriculture officer.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Plant resistant hybrids or varieties where available; this is the cheapest control.
Keep a watch on the crop in cool, wet weather.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if most leaves carry pustules before the crop is near maturity.

sources.title: Common Rust on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension
Corn Rusts: Common and Southern Rust - NC State Extension

name: Smut
summary: A fungus disease that makes swollen, fleshy galls (tumour-like growths) on ears, tassels, stalks and leaves of corn. Dark spore powder fills the galls when they dry.
symptoms: Thick, fleshy galls, first covered in a white to silvery skin, on ears, stalks, tassels or leaves.
Galls on leaves usually stay small and look like blisters.
As galls ripen they turn dark inside, then dry and burst, releasing black dusty spores.
Early infection can cause yellowing and rippling of leaf tissue near the galls.
causes: Caused by the fungus Ustilago maydis. Its thick-walled spores live for several years in soil and crop residue.
Wind and splashing rain or irrigation water carry spores to plants; the fungus enters through wounds or silks.
Hail, wind or machine damage to young plants, and heat or drought that gives poor pollination, make it worse.
Too much nitrogen fertilizer and wet weather can also favour it.

actions.text: Check ears, tassels and stalks for galls. Field corn rarely loses much, so do not overspend on control.
Take care not to wound young plants during weeding and other field work, because wounds let the fungus in.
Rotate to another crop and keep soil fertility balanced; avoid too much nitrogen.

prevention: Plant resistant hybrids or varieties where available.
Rotate crops and keep soil fertility balanced; avoid excess nitrogen.
Clear crop residue after harvest.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if many ears in the field carry galls.

sources.title: Common Smut on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension
Common Smut of Corn - University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension

name: Bacterial Blight
summary: A bacterial disease that makes small angular spots with yellow halos on soybean leaves. It usually stays at low levels and seldom cuts yield much.
symptoms: Small angular water-soaked spots that turn yellow, then brown, as the leaf tissue dies.
Dark spots are ringed by a yellowish-green halo.
Spots join into large dead patches, and the dead tissue may fall out, leaving ragged leaves.
Seen most on young leaves in the upper part of the plant. Stems, pods and seed can also be infected.
causes: Caused by a bacterium, Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea (also written Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. glycinea).
It survives in crop residue and can be carried on seed.
Wind and rain spread it, and so does working in the field while leaves are wet.
Cool, wet, windy weather favours it; hot, dry weather stops it.

actions.text: Do not walk through or work in the field while the leaves are wet.
Check young upper leaves after windy, rainy spells for angular spots with yellow halos.
Do not save seed from a field that had this disease.
Chemical sprays are not the main answer; ask your agriculture officer if the disease is severe.

prevention: Use clean, disease-free seed.
Plant resistant varieties.
Rotate with crops such as corn or small grains, which this bacterium does not infect.
Bury or clear crop residue after a diseased crop.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if the disease returns in most seasons or is severe.

sources.title: Bacterial Blight on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension
Bacterial Blight of Soybean - Crop Protection Network

name: Brown Spot
summary: A common fungus leaf disease of soybean, also called Septoria brown spot. It starts on lower leaves, can make leaves drop early, and seldom causes big yield loss.
symptoms: Small dark brown spots on the lowest leaves first, which later move up the plant.
Spots grow and join into irregular brown patches, often with yellow areas beside them.
Leaves turn yellow, then rusty brown, and may drop early.
Spots can also be seen on stems and pods. It can look like soybean rust, but brown spot has no raised pustules or spores under the leaf.
causes: Caused by the fungus Septoria glycines, which lives on soybean residue left from the last crop and may travel on seed.
Spores are moved by wind and splashing rain.
Favoured by warm, wet weather with at least 6 hours of leaf wetness.
Worse when soybean is grown year after year in the same field, especially with little ploughing.

actions.text: Check lower leaves early in the season and see whether spots are climbing up the plant.
If the disease is heavy, bury soybean residue after harvest so it rots faster.
Rotate out of soybean for at least one year in fields where the disease keeps getting worse.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Rotate soybean with other crops, not other legumes.
Bury crop residue in fields with heavy infection.
Pick varieties that tolerate the disease better; none is fully resistant.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if you cannot tell brown spot from soybean rust.

sources.title: Septoria Brown Spot in Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension
Septoria Brown Spot of Soybean - University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension

name: Downy Mildew
summary: A disease caused by a fungus-like organism that makes pale yellow spots on top of soybean leaves and grey fuzzy growth underneath. It is usually harmless to yield.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper side of young leaves, which are not water-soaked.
Old spots merge into large irregular brown patches with yellow-green edges.
Tan to gray fuzzy tufts on the underside of the leaf, mostly in humid, wet weather such as early morning.
Infected seed may be small, dull white or cracked, with a whitish crust of spores inside the pod.
causes: Caused by Peronospora manshurica, a fungus-like organism (an oomycete).
It survives on infected leaves and on seed, and seed can carry it to the next crop.
Dew, high humidity and mild temperatures favour it, and it is most common once flowering begins.
Older leaves resist better and hotter midseason weather usually stops it.

actions.text: Check upper young leaves for yellow spots and the underside for grey fuzz, mainly in humid weather.
Bury infested residue after harvest where disease was severe.
Do not keep seed from a field with heavily infected pods.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties; many sources of resistance exist.
Rotate soybean with a non-bean crop for at least one year.
Use clean seed.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if many plants show spots before flowering ends.

sources.title: Downy Mildew on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension
Downy Mildew of Soybean - Crop Protection Network

name: Frog Eye Leaf Spot
summary: A fungus disease of soybean that makes small spots with a reddish-brown or purple ring, like a frog's eye. It spreads in warm, humid weather and can cause leaf drop.
symptoms: Small dark, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown or gray with a reddish-brown or purple ring.
Older spot centres turn light gray or white with tiny black specks, or fall out leaving a shot-hole look.
Spots can join into large damaged areas and leaves may drop early.
Spots can also be on stems, pods and seed. Young leaves near the top are hit most.
causes: Caused by the fungus Cercospora sojina, which survives on crop residue and in seed.
Rain splash carries spores from residue up to young leaves, and new spores form on the spots all season.
Warm, humid and long wet spells favour it, usually after flowering.
Infection at or before flowering causes the biggest loss; late infection matters little.

actions.text: Check young upper leaves for spots with reddish-brown or purple rings, from flowering onward.
In fields with heavy disease, bury soybean residue; if that is not possible, rotate to another crop.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
Do not save seed from a field with heavy disease.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Use disease-free seed.
Rotate soybean with a non-bean crop.
Do not plant soybean into infested residue.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spots appear before or around flowering on susceptible varieties.

sources.title: Frogeye Leaf Spot on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension
Frogeye Leaf Spot of Soybean - Ohio State University Extension

name: Mosaic
summary: A virus disease of soybean that mottles and crinkles the leaves. It can stunt plants and spoil seed quality. There is no cure once a plant is infected.
symptoms: Leaves show light and dark green mottling, mostly on young fast-growing leaves.
Leaf blades may pucker along the veins and curl downward, or look blistered and distorted.
Infected plants may be stunted with fewer pods and smaller seeds.
Seed can be mottled, which lowers grain quality and germination. Symptoms fade in very hot weather.
causes: Caused by Soybean mosaic virus, a virus that lives inside the plant.
Infected seed is the most important way it enters a field.
Aphids spread it from plant to plant, and it can also spread through plant sap.
Plants infected when young show more symptoms.

actions.text: Use only clean seed; do not plant seed saved from fields where plants were mottled.
Look for mottled, crinkled young leaves, and for aphids on the plants.
Spraying for aphids does not reliably stop this virus; ask your agriculture officer before spending money on it.

prevention: Plant seed that is free of the virus.
Plant early, which may help.
Choose varieties with some resistance where available.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if many young plants show mottled, crinkled leaves.

sources.title: Soybean Mosaic Virus - University of Minnesota Extension
Soybean Mosaic of Soybean - Crop Protection Network

name: Rust
summary: A fast-spreading fungus disease of soybean that causes leaf spots and early leaf drop. Under favourable conditions it can cause very heavy yield loss.
symptoms: Tan or reddish-brown spots, first on the underside of lower leaves.
Small blister-like pustules form in the spots, then burst and release tan spores.
Spots and pustules can also be on pods and stems; a hand lens helps to see them.
Heavy attack causes leaf drop.
causes: Caused by the rust fungus Phakopsora pachyrhizi, which survives only on living green plants.
Its spores are carried by wind, sometimes over long distances.
Favoured by long wet weather, moderate temperatures and high humidity, and most common at and after flowering.
Early spots, before pustules form, look like other common leaf diseases.

actions.text: Check lower leaves every week, especially in wet weather after flowering starts.
Look at the underside of leaves with a hand lens for pustules and tell your agriculture officer early.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Early scouting is the key. Early sowing in a season has been seen to suffer less damage in Indian trials.
Ask your agriculture office which varieties are better for your area, since resistant ones are limited.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer at once if you see rusty spots on the underside of leaves.
